paras: The flogging and shooting of Jim Strickland was a mob attack on a Black man in Henry County, Georgia, reported in a dispatch from Griffin dated August 18, 1900. A crowd gave Strickland 150 lashes and shot him four times, accusing him of threatening talk against white people; he was not expected to die. The Associated Press story ran in papers from Georgia to Maine under headlines that ranged from "Flogged For Threatening Whites" to "Worse Than Savages."

According to the dispatch, Strickland had been "using highly incendiary talk, saying what he would do if a white man crossed his path," and was regarded as a "firebrand" in his community. The same report said he had been "repeatedly warned to modify his language and actions" and that the warnings had no effect. These charges appear only in the wire account, which gave no source for them and no reply from Strickland.

A crowd took Strickland out and gave him 150 lashes on the bare back. They then shot him once in the arm, twice in the thigh and once in the leg. The dispatch said that "the mob went about its work quietly but effectively" and did not name any of its members or give their number.

After the attack Strickland was taken to the house of a Black resident, where his injuries were treated, and it was "not thought that he will die." No report of arrests, an investigation or any later word on Strickland's condition appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers only through the Associated Press dispatch, which appeared on August 19 in the Raleigh News & Observer, the Savannah Morning News and the Richmond Times. The Portland Daily Press in Maine carried a shortened version on August 20, the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic reprinted the News & Observer item on August 21, and the Poplarville Free Press in Mississippi ran it on August 23. The wire text itself repeated the attackers' grievance as fact and called Strickland "the unfortunate wretch."

Headlines varied more than the text beneath them. The News & Observer led with the accusation, "Flogged For Threatening Whites," while the Savannah Morning News paired "Whipped and Shot a Negro" with the explanation "The Man Had Been Using Highly Objectionable Language." The Richmond Times used the plain "Given 150 Lashes," and the Portland paper chose "How They Tamed Strickland." Only the Poplarville Free Press dissented, heading the story "Worse Than Savages. Cruel Treatment of a Negro Charged With Incendiary Language" and prefacing the accusation with "It is stated that." No Black-press coverage of the attack was found.

accounts.label: Associated Press dispatch from Griffin
accounts.gist: A crowd whipped and shot Strickland because he had used 'incendiary talk' against whites and ignored repeated warnings; the mob worked 'quietly but effectively' and he was not expected to die. The reasons given come only from the attackers' side as relayed by the wire.

accounts.label: Poplarville Free Press reprint
accounts.gist: The same text, but the accusation is distanced with 'It is stated that' and the episode is headed 'Worse Than Savages' and 'Cruel Treatment'.

framing.detail: The Raleigh News & Observer headed the AP item 'Flogged For Threatening Whites', putting the accusation first; its weekly, the Farmer and Mechanic, reprinted it unchanged.
The Savannah Morning News headline 'Whipped and Shot a Negro' carried the deck 'The Man Had Been Using Highly Objectionable Language', presenting the mob's reason as the explanation.
The Richmond Times used the bare headline 'Given 150 Lashes'.
The Portland Daily Press headed a shortened version 'How They Tamed Strickland', adopting the attackers' view of the whipping as taming.
The Poplarville Free Press headed the story 'Worse Than Savages. Cruel Treatment of a Negro Charged With Incendiary Language' and qualified the accusation as hearsay.
